name: GHC/Haskell
summary: A non-strict, statically polymorphic functional language and the Glasgow Haskell Compiler, whose module-oriented compiler lowers Haskell through Core and STG representations into native or alternative backends.
scope: static polymorphic types and type classes

features.name: Non-strict polymorphic language model
features.description: The Haskell report describes a purely functional language with non-strict semantics, static polymorphic typing, algebraic datatypes, pattern matching, type classes, and monadic I/O.
benefits: Separates pure expression structure from explicit I/O effects
Provides reusable abstractions through polymorphism and algebraic data
costs: Non-strict evaluation makes resource and termination behavior less direct to predict
Type-class overloading and lazy values add semantic machinery to compilation and runtime

features.name: Module-oriented dependency and interface build
features.description: GHC's make mode follows imports from root modules, recompiles modules that are out of date, emits object and interface files, and can compile independent modules in parallel.
benefits: Derives compilation order from source dependencies
Provides reusable interface artifacts and parallel build opportunities
costs: Module interfaces and dependency freshness become build-state concerns
Parallel compilation still depends on dependency closure and available resources

features.name: Core, STG, and backend compilation pipeline
features.description: GHC organizes compilation into distinct phases and source modules include front-end, Haskell-to-Core, Core-to-STG, STG-to-Cmm, and backend/code-output boundaries. The user guide documents multiple code-generation backends and phase control.
benefits: Provides intermediate boundaries for optimization and runtime-oriented lowering
Allows code generation to target different backend strategies
costs: Each representation and lowering boundary adds invariants and maintenance cost
Source-level behavior must remain explainable across several transformed representations

features.name: Capability-based concurrent runtime
features.description: GHC's runtime models physical parallelism with capabilities. The threaded runtime can run Haskell threads across multiple capabilities, and foreign calls can allow other Haskell threads to continue while the call is in progress.
benefits: Makes available parallel execution capacity an explicit runtime setting
Separates Haskell-thread scheduling from the OS-thread pool used around foreign calls
costs: Runtime flags and foreign-call annotations affect concurrency behavior
Parallel evaluation introduces blackholing, scheduling, and shared-runtime state

mathematical_views.question: How do typed expressions, non-strict evaluation, algebraic values, and bottom relate in a Haskell program?
assumptions: Expressions are typed terms and evaluation may defer subterms
Bottom represents undefined or nonterminating computation in the abstract semantics
The view abstracts implementation-specific optimizations and runtime representation

mathematical_views.question: How do imports, interface files, and out-of-date checks determine GHC compilation order and parallelism?
assumptions: Modules are vertices and imports are directed edges
A module can be compiled when required dependencies and interfaces are available
The view abstracts package databases, generated code, and build-system integration

mathematical_views.question: How does GHC lower a Haskell module through Core and STG-oriented representations toward code generation?
assumptions: Each intermediate representation is a node in a directed refinement relation
Lowering preserves the program properties relevant to the next compiler phase
The view is a candidate abstraction and does not prove compiler correctness

mathematical_views.question: How do runnable Haskell threads, capabilities, foreign calls, and runtime scheduling transitions determine concurrent execution?
assumptions: Capabilities are execution resources and Haskell threads are schedulable work items
Foreign-call transitions may release a capability for other work
The model abstracts OS scheduler behavior and does not claim a particular fairness guarantee

benefits: Expressive pure abstractions and deferred computation
costs: Laziness and overloading complicate resource and runtime reasoning
Interfaces and freshness add build-state complexity

benefits: Specialized compiler phases and backend choices
Explicit runtime capacity for concurrent execution
costs: Scheduling, foreign calls, and blackholing complicate runtime behavior
